analysis.one_liner: Blocks agencies and courts from penalizing anyone for violating a rule that wasn't clearly published or didn't give fair warning.
analysis.headline: The bill won approval from a House Judiciary subcommittee by voice vote but never received a full committee markup or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stop federal agencies and courts from imposing fines or other penalties for violating a federal regulation if any one of three things is true: the rule wasn't printed in the Code of Federal Regulations or Federal Register, wasn't known, and couldn't reasonably have been discovered; the rule didn't give a reasonable person clear warning of what it forbids or requires; or the person reasonably relied on a written answer from the agency about what the rule means. [S2][S3] The stated purpose is due process — no one should be punished for breaking a rule they couldn't know. [S3] The practical effect would be to give anyone facing a federal penalty a new legal defense, which matters most to the businesses and entities that are the usual targets of regulatory enforcement. [S2][S3] The bill never advanced past a House Judiciary subcommittee. [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: Regulated businesses facing fines, penalties, or enforcement actions gain the most: the 'fair warning' and reliance-on-guidance defenses give them grounds to challenge or escape sanctions after the fact. Ordinary people also gain something real — anyone fined under an unpublished, obscure, or vague rule, or misled by a government official's written answer, could avoid the penalty. But because businesses are overwhelmingly the ones penalized for regulatory violations, the defense's value concentrates on regulated industry.

how_it_helps.text: An agency or court could not impose any sanction for violating a rule if the rule was not printed in the Code of Federal Regulations or the Federal Register, was not known to the person, and was not knowable through a reasonable, good-faith investigation of the applicable rules. [S2][S3]
No sanction could be imposed if the rule failed to give fair warning — defined as a rule a reasonable person acting in good faith could identify with reasonable certainty. [S2][S3]

For penalties applied after the fact, no sanction could be imposed on a person who reasonably relied in writing on an agency's or authorized official's statement about what the rule prohibits or requires. [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: The public protected by federal regulation bears the cost when enforcement gets harder: a penalty that becomes contestable after the fact is a penalty that gets delayed, reduced, or dropped, which weakens the deterrent behind health, safety, environmental, financial, and consumer rules. Agencies would also face more litigation over every sanction they try to impose. Anyone the rules protect — workers, consumers, communities near polluting facilities — absorbs that erosion.

drawbacks.text: The 'fair warning' exception is open-ended: because it covers any rule a reasonable person could not identify 'with reasonable certainty,' nearly any sanctioned party could argue the rule was vague and force the agency into court, turning routine enforcement into litigation. [S3]

The bill's own findings acknowledge that federal regulations protect the environment and the health and safety of all Americans; making those rules' penalties easier to escape weakens the enforcement that produces that protection. [S3]

A genuine due-process concern is real: people and small entities can be penalized under rules they had no realistic way to learn. The bill addresses that, but the same defense is available to the largest regulated firms, who have compliance staff and would use it as standard practice. [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The fair-warning principle the bill invokes is legitimate — punishing someone for breaking a rule they could not know is genuinely unfair. But the bill is drafted broadly rather than narrowly: instead of a targeted fix for unpublished or genuinely ambiguous rules, it creates a general post-hoc defense available to any penalized party, and the parties positioned to use it systematically are large regulated firms facing fines. The due-process gain for ordinary people is modest; the enforcement cost is diffuse but real, spread across every area of federal regulation.

outcome.mechanism: A House Judiciary subcommittee held a hearing and approved an amended version by voice vote, but the full committee never marked it up and the House never voted on it before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. George Gekas (R-PA) introduced the bill on March 1, 1999 with 13 original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee. [S3][S5]
The bill attracted 26 cosponsors in total: 21 Republicans and 5 Democrats. [S4]
It was referred to the Judiciary Subcommittee on Commercial and Administrative Law on March 18, 1999, which held a hearing on June 29, 1999. [S5]

On September 29, 1999 the subcommittee considered and marked up the bill and forwarded it to the full committee in amended form by voice vote — but the record shows no further committee action, no committee vote, and no House floor vote for the rest of the 106th Congress. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal agencies came out ahead: their existing authority to enforce rules — including rules that are obscure or loosely worded — remained intact, and the public kept the full deterrent of regulatory penalties. Businesses that would have gained a new defense against sanctions got nothing, since the rules they operate under were left unchanged too.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal agencies and the rules they enforce

industries.industry: Regulated industries (manufacturers, energy and chemical firms, financial and other federally regulated businesses)
industries.note: These firms are the usual targets of federal regulatory fines, so the fair-warning and agency-guidance defenses would let them contest or escape sanctions that now stick. Their gain comes directly at the cost of the deterrent behind the rules protecting workers, consumers, and communities.

industries.industry: People and small businesses facing obscure federal rules
industries.note: Individuals and small entities fined under unpublished, hard-to-find, or genuinely vague rules — or misled by a government official's written answer — would have a defense. This is the bill's genuine pro-public side, though large firms are positioned to use the same defense far more often.

An open-ended 'fair warning' defense available in every enforcement case creates a new stream of challenge litigation, which firms facing penalties would pay for and which agencies would have to defend against.
